title: A guest lecture on light pollution

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Tom and Nina, discussing a guest lecture on light pollution and some resources for a seminar. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Did you enjoy the guest lecture on light pollution on Monday? I thought it was one of the best we've had this term.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Me too. I'd expected it to be mostly about astronomers who can't see the stars any more, but it was much broader than that.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: The photos she'd taken herself were stunning, weren't they? Especially the ones of the city from the hills at night.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: They were beautiful, but to be honest they didn't really teach me anything. What stayed with me was the way she compared different cities, and showed how some are far brighter at night than others of the same size.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Yes, that part changed my thinking too. I'd always assumed big cities were more or less the same, and they're really not.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: She did a short section on the history of street lighting as well.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: She did, but she rushed through it, so it didn't make much of an impression on me. And her tips on what we can do at home, like closing the curtains and switching off garden lights, were sensible enough, but nothing I hadn't heard before.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: No. For me, the most powerful part was how artificial light affects animals. I had no idea that so many moths and other insects die around street lamps, or that baby sea turtles sometimes crawl towards bright lights instead of the sea.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: That really got to me as well. I've looked at outside lights quite differently since then.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: And what about the project she described at the end, in that small town that replaced all its street lights?

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: That impressed me. Mind you, it wasn't exactly quick. She said it took nearly six years from the first public meeting to the last new lamp.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: True. But the savings were remarkable. The town's electricity bill for street lighting fell by more than half, and they've spent that money on other things.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Mm. And people weren't all in favour at the beginning, were they? Quite a few residents complained that the streets would feel unsafe.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: That's right. And she was honest that there isn't enough evidence yet to say whether crime has gone up or down.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: What I loved was that the local primary schools took part. The children went out at night with their parents and counted the stars they could see, before and after the change.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Yes, that was a lovely idea. It's a clever way to get whole families interested, too.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Anyway, shall we go through the resources on the reading list for Thursday's seminar? We're supposed to say what we think of each one.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Sure. Let's start with the article on street lighting and insects.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: I found it really hard going. The research behind it seems solid, but it's written for other scientists. Every other word was a technical term, and I kept having to stop and look things up.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Same here. I gave up halfway through and just read the summary. What about the documentary on dark-sky parks? I watched it last night.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: So did I. It's quite recent, so at least it's up to date. The presenter's commentary was a bit flat, though.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Yes, but the filming of the night sky was incredible. Those time-lapse shots of the Milky Way are what make it worth watching.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Then there's the podcast about light and sleep. Did you get anything out of that?

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Not really. The presenter mostly talked about her own sleep problems, and the guests did the same. It was all 'this happened to me', with hardly any mention of actual research.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: I felt the same. It's a shame, because it's such an important topic. The report on LED street lamps was more serious, I thought.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: It was carefully researched, and I don't think it exaggerated the problem at all. But it came out quite a few years ago, and a lot of its figures on costs have changed since then, so I wouldn't rely on them.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Good point. And the book on stargazing? I only read the chapter on skyglow.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: That chapter was the best part. I'd never understood how a city can light up the sky miles away, but the way it explains light bouncing off tiny particles in the air finally made sense to me.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: Mm, it's the clearest account I've read. Finally, the website with the brightness map. Someone told me it only covers Europe, but in fact it shows the whole world. I spent ages zooming in on our own street.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Me too! The map's fun, but the useful part is the page of suggestions underneath. It tells you which kind of bulb to buy and how to point outdoor lights downwards, and I've already changed the light by our front door.

lines.speaker: NINA
lines.text: I might do the same. Right, shall we start writing up our notes?

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 3.

groups.stem: Which TWO parts of the lecture on light pollution had the greatest effect on the students?
Which TWO things about the town's lighting project impressed the students?

options.text: the part played by local schoolchildren
the short time it took to complete
the support it had from residents
the amount of money it saved

groups.instructions: What do the students think about each of the following resources? Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 25–30.
groups.title: Opinions

options.text: It uses too much technical language.
Some of its information is out of date.
It makes the problem seem worse than it is.
It relies on personal experience rather than research.
Its pictures are its strongest feature.
It explains a difficult idea clearly.
It covers too small an area.

items.text: Article on street lighting and insects

evidence.quote: What stayed with me was the way she compared different cities

pairs: had the greatest effect
What stayed with me … that part changed my thinking
the comparison between cities
the way she compared different cities
21.why: Nina says the comparison of cities stayed with her, and Tom agrees it changed his thinking (B). The other answer is E (see question 22).
21.trap: Tom praises the photos (A), but Nina says they didn't teach her anything, and Tom does not disagree.

evidence.quote: For me, the most powerful part was how artificial light affects animals.

pairs: the effects on wildlife
how artificial light affects animals … moths … sea turtles
22.why: Nina calls the part about animals the most powerful, and Tom says it 'really got to me as well' (E). B and E can go in either order.
22.trap: The history (C) 'didn't make much of an impression', and the home tips (D) were 'nothing I hadn't heard before'.

pairs: impressed
remarkable
the amount of money it saved
the savings … electricity bill … fell by more than half
23.why: Nina finds the savings remarkable: the electricity bill fell by more than half (D). The other answer is A (see question 24).
23.trap: B is wrong: Tom says 'it wasn't exactly quick', as it took nearly six years.

evidence.quote: What I loved was that the local primary schools took part.

pairs: impressed
What I loved … a lovely idea
the part played by local schoolchildren
the local primary schools took part … The children … counted the stars
24.why: Tom loved the way the primary schools took part, and Nina calls it a lovely idea (A). A and D can go in either order.
24.trap: Many residents complained at first, so C is wrong. There isn't enough evidence about crime yet, so E is wrong.

evidence.quote: Every other word was a technical term

pairs: too much technical language
Every other word was a technical term … written for other scientists
25.why: Nina had to keep looking words up because the article is full of technical terms.
25.trap: She says the research 'seems solid', so the problem is not the evidence. It is the language.

evidence.quote: the filming of the night sky was incredible

pairs: its strongest feature
what make it worth watching
Its pictures
the filming of the night sky … time-lapse shots
26.why: Tom says the filming is incredible and is what makes the documentary worth watching. That is its strongest feature.
26.trap: B is wrong: the documentary is recent and up to date. The commentary is weak, but that is not one of the options.

evidence.quote: It was all 'this happened to me', with hardly any mention of actual research.

pairs: personal experience
her own sleep problems … 'this happened to me'
rather than research
hardly any mention of actual research
27.why: The presenter and guests talked about their own experiences and hardly mentioned research.

evidence.quote: it came out quite a few years ago, and a lot of its figures on costs have changed since then

pairs: out of date
came out quite a few years ago … have changed since then
Some of its information
a lot of its figures on costs
28.why: The report is old, and its cost figures have changed since it was written.
28.trap: Tom says it did not exaggerate the problem, so C is wrong. Listen for 'But', which often brings the real point.

evidence.quote: the way it explains light bouncing off tiny particles in the air finally made sense to me

pairs: a difficult idea
I'd never understood how a city can light up the sky
explains … clearly
finally made sense to me … the clearest account
29.why: Tom had never understood skyglow before, but the book's explanation finally made sense, and Nina calls it the clearest account she has read.

evidence.quote: the useful part is the page of suggestions underneath

pairs: useful practical advice
the useful part is the page of suggestions … which kind of bulb to buy
30.why: The website gives suggestions such as which bulb to buy and how to point lights down, and Tom has already followed them.
30.trap: H is wrong: someone said the map only covers Europe, but in fact it shows the whole world.
